title: Episode 92: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
itunes_title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
description:
**Monday Immune Engager** — our weekly pick from the latest immune-engager digest.

**[Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11176-1)**

*Nature, 2026*

DOI: [10.1038/s41586-026-11176-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11176-1)

**Question:** Can IL-10 receptor agonism be made to suppress myeloid cells without also activating T cells, which drives IL-10's clinical toxicity?

**Answer:** A tetravalent nanobody agonist (lead E07/A05) suppresses macrophage TNF/IL-6 with low-picomolar potency while leaving T cells silent, via a binding geometry that makes signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and sensitive to receptor density. Evidence comes from structures, cell assays and a single-dose cynomolgus study, not chronic dosing or human data.

**Three takeaways**

1. Myeloid cells tolerate TYK2 loss and still suppress TNF/IL-6; T cells require TYK2 for any granzyme B/IFN-γ response.
2. One of 882 nanobody combinations gave myeloid-selective agonism; linker and topology swaps show selectivity depends on geometry, not just binding.
3. Selectivity is receptor-density-gated — reversible by overexpressing IL-10Rα on T cells, or redirected to T/NK cells using an IL-2Rγ arm.

source_metadata.title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
source_metadata.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities
                    1–5
                    . Here we show that myeloid and T cells differ in their dependence on JAK-family kinase pairing for IL-10 signalling and function. We took advantage of this differential kinase dependence to engineer a tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist (msIL-10R agonist) that fully recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells. Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases.
